text.text: Every job on one board: clients, productions from brief to delivery, the shot list for each shoot, crew and gear bookings, and the cuts waiting on feedback. Check the Dashboard before each shoot day, tick shots off as they are captured and keep Cuts waiting on client honest.
Clients
The companies and organizations the studio makes video for.
Productions
Each video job from brief through delivery.
Shot list
Every planned shot, ticked off on the shoot day.
Bookings
Crew, gear, locations and talent booked for each production.
Cuts
Each edit version sent to the client, with its review status.

This workspace runs a video production company: clients, each production from brief to delivery with its budget, the shot list, the crew, gear and locations booked for each shoot, and every cut sent for client feedback. Edit files and footage live on your drives and editing software; this is where the job is planned and tracked.

Ironbark's factory story is past its delivery date with version two in revisions. The client wants a bigger logo, a shorter safety section and a different founder take, so the editor turns it around in a day and the producer explains this was the last included round.

How to read the numbers

cells.text: Shots captured divided by shots planned
Under 100 after the shoot day means schedule pickups now
Budget minus the cost of bookings
Negative before post starts means talk to the client about scope
Cuts in client review or revisions
More than two per production means chase and set a firm feedback date
Under seven with open revisions means clear the calendar for the edit

text.text: Most problems on a shoot day were decided in pre-production. A complete plan makes the day calm, and calm days produce better footage.
Two weeks before the shoot
Brief signed off: audience, message, length and every deliverable
Treatment or storyboard approved by the client
Shot list written: every shot with size, location and notes
Locations confirmed, with access times and parking
Crew booked: camera, sound, lighting, drone if needed
Gear booked, and insurance certificates received for rentals
Release forms prepared for everyone on camera and every private location
Music direction agreed; a licensed track or a composer booked
One week before
Recce every location you have not shot before: light at the shoot time, power, noise, where the crew can set up.
Confirm every booking.
Bookings not confirmed
on the production should read zero.
Write the call sheet: times, addresses, contacts, weather, nearest hospital.
Send the shot list to the client and ask what is a must-have.
Interviews
Send the interviewee the topics, not the questions, two days before.
Ask them to avoid fine stripes and bright white.
Book a quiet room; turn off air conditioning and fridges during takes.
Permits and safety

cells.text: City film permit if your crew blocks the path
A licensed pilot and permission for the airspace
The client's safety induction and protective gear

text.text: Example

The Delta Heritage oral history shoot is in pre-production. The museum archive room is confirmed but the sound recordist is still only requested, so the producer confirms or replaces them before the end of the week.
Client on set
Agree who from the client attends and what they decide on the day. One decision-maker on set saves hours; three opinions on every take cost the schedule.
Budget check
Before the shoot, compare crew and gear costs with the budget. If
Budget left
is thin, cut a day or a camera now, not in the edit.
A shoot day runs on the call sheet and the shot list. Everyone knows the plan, the producer protects the time, and nothing leaves the location until the footage is backed up.
Before call time
Gear checked the night before: batteries charged, cards formatted, lenses clean
Call sheet sent to crew and client
Release forms and pens in the kit
Water, food and a first-aid kit
On set
Safety briefing first, especially on factory floors and sites.
Shoot the must-have shots first, while energy and light are best.
Mark each shot
Captured
as you get it. A shot that failed becomes
Pickup needed
with a note on why.
Record room tone for 30 seconds at each location.
Get a signed release from everyone on camera before they leave.
The producer's job on the day
Keep the schedule: call time, setups, lunch, wrap.
Talk to the client so the director can work.
Decide quickly when a shot is not working: move on and come back if there is time.
Wrap
Every card backed up to two drives before anyone leaves
Shot list checked: everything captured or marked for pickup
Location left as found; photos of how it was left
Bookings marked
Wrapped
After the shoot
Send the client a short note: what you captured and any pickups needed.
Log any overtime or extra gear so the budget stays true.
Common problems

cells.text: Record dialogue in a pause; shoot inserts during noise
Shoot wides first, then close-ups under your own light
Start with easy questions; roll from the start

text.text: Example
On the Sutter Valley shoot, the label close-up was soft. It is marked Pickup needed, and the producer books a short pickup with the bottling line the same day as the colour session.
Post-production is where budgets disappear, usually through feedback that arrives late, in pieces, or from too many people. A clear round structure protects the edit and the client relationship.
The stages

cells.text: Story and structure; no grading or final sound
Locked story; pacing and shot choices

Send one link with frame-accurate commenting, plus three questions you want answered.

Client review
and the sent date.
Feedback rules
One person collects feedback from everyone on the client side and sends it as one list.
Feedback within three working days, or the schedule moves.
Write the notes in
Client notes
so the editor works from one place.

Archive
Keep project files and footage for at least a year. Clients come back for new cutdowns, and a quick turnaround from your archive is easy, welcome work.
Example

The Sutter Valley autumn film is due this week and the first assembly is still with the client. The producer calls for notes the same day, agrees a short extension in writing, and holds the social cutdowns until the main film is approved so the verticals are not cut twice.
Keep the edit moving
When feedback is late, send a friendly reminder on day three and a call on day five. Tell the client plainly how the delivery date moves if notes do not arrive.
A good quote is clear about what is included, how many days, how many rounds, and what costs extra. Most disputes start with a quote that left those things vague.
Ask before you price
Where will the video run, and how long should it be?
Which deliverables: main film, vertical, square, captions?
How many locations and how many people on camera?
Does the client supply music, or do we license it?
What is the deadline, and what drives it?
Building the price

cells.text: Producer days for brief, treatment, recce and planning
Crew day rates times shoot days, plus gear
Editor days, colour, sound mix, motion graphics
Licence fee for the uses agreed

text.text: Enter the total as the
Budget
on the production and book crew and gear against it.
The quote document
Deliverables, listed one by one.
Shoot days and locations.
Edit rounds included
, and the price of an extra round.
Payment terms: often half to book, half on delivery.
What happens if the shoot is postponed or the weather fails.
Pricing mistakes to avoid
Forgetting travel days, parking and meals.
Pricing post as a fixed number of hours with no round limit.
Leaving out captions and vertical versions, which every client now wants.
Not charging for pickups caused by client changes.
After the job
Compare the real crew and gear costs and edit days with the quote. Note what ran over, and price the next similar job with that in mind.
Example

Ironbark's safety training cutdowns are in brief. The producer prices one shoot day on the factory floor, two editor days, captions and three vertical cutdowns, with one edit round included, because the client already knows the style from the factory story.
